nodes.label: The Ottoman state
nodes.full: Istanbul: it held the Hejaz for the legitimacy of the caliphal guardianship, paid for it with the Sürre and the caravan subsidies, arbitrated the sharifs' quarrels, and under Abdülhamid II made it the centrepiece of a pan-Islamic policy.
nodes.src: background — Faroqhi, 'Pilgrims and Sultans' (1994); Ochsenwald (1984).

nodes.label: The First Saudi State
nodes.full: The Wahhābī–Saudi power of Najd: it occupied Mecca and Medina from 1803, stopped the Ottoman Hajj and demolished the shrines, and its containment became a fixed Ottoman priority for a century.
nodes.src: background — Burckhardt (1830); the Saudi chronicles.

nodes.label: Muḥammad ʿAlī's Egypt
nodes.full: The Egyptian viceroy who, on the sultan's order, retook the Hejaz from the Saudis and then administered it until 1840, introducing a garrison and a firmer hand as a preview of direct Ottoman rule.
nodes.src: background — Fahmy, 'All the Pasha's Men' (1997).

nodes.label: The European empires
nodes.full: Britain, France and the Netherlands: masters of most of the world's Muslims, watching the Hajj through their Jeddah consulates, pressing on the slave trade, imposing the sanitary regime, and colliding with the closed Hejaz at Jeddah in 1858.
nodes.src: background — Slight, 'The British Empire and the Hajj' (2015).

nodes.label: Steam and cholera
nodes.full: The technology and the disease that together remade the Hajj: the steamship that carried hundreds of thousands to Jeddah, and the cholera that travelled with them and turned the pilgrimage into an international health emergency.
nodes.src: background — Valeska Huber on the sanitary conferences.

nodes.label: The Ottoman guardianship begins
nodes.full: After Selim I took Egypt, the sharif Barakāt II sent his son to submit. The Ottomans confirmed the sharif in office, assumed the guardianship of the two holy cities, and took over the kiswa, the grain and the organisation of the pilgrim caravans.
nodes.src: al-Nahrawālī, al-Iʿlām bi-aʿlām bayt Allāh al-ḥarām; Suraiya Faroqhi, 'Pilgrims and Sultans: The Hajj under the Ottomans' (1994).

nodes.label: The sharifs of Mecca under the Ottomans
nodes.full: The Qatādid dynasty continued, its Dhawū Zayd and Dhawū Barakāt branches feuding for the emirate, with Istanbul confirming, deposing and occasionally sending troops to impose a sharif of its choice.
nodes.src: Faroqhi, 'Pilgrims and Sultans' (1994); the Ottoman records of sharifian appointments.

nodes.label: The Sürre and the privileged province
nodes.full: The Hejaz paid no tax. Instead Istanbul sent the annual Sürre — a caravan of money and grain for the mosques, the sharif, the scholars and the poor — and organised and subsidised the Damascus and Egyptian Hajj caravans. The province was governed as a trust.
nodes.src: the Sürre registers in the Ottoman archives; Faroqhi (1994).

nodes.label: The First Saudi State takes the Hejaz
nodes.full: The Wahhābī–Saudi forces took Ṭāʾif, Mecca and Medina, expelled the Ottoman-backed sharif, stopped the imperial Hajj, demolished the domed tombs of the Baqīʿ, and imposed the doctrine — the gravest challenge to the Ottoman guardianship in three centuries.
nodes.src: Burckhardt, 'Notes on the Bedouins and Wahábys' (1830); the Saudi chronicles.

nodes.label: The Egyptian reconquest and administration
nodes.full: On the sultan's order, Egyptian armies under Ṭūsūn and Ibrāhīm Pasha retook the Hejaz from the Saudis. Egypt then administered the province, restored the sharifate and the sanctuary practice, and held it until the 1840 settlement forced its withdrawal.
nodes.src: Burckhardt, 'Travels in Arabia' (1829); the Egyptian sources on the Hejaz administration.

nodes.label: Direct rule and the Vilayet of the Hejaz
nodes.full: After Egypt left, the Ottomans reasserted direct control, created the Vilayet of the Hejaz in 1872 under a governor at Jeddah, and kept the sharif as a subordinate — a tighter grip driven by the Wahhābī scare and by the province's new value for the pan-Islamic policy of Abdülhamid II.
nodes.src: William Ochsenwald, 'Religion, Society, and the State in Arabia: The Hijaz under Ottoman Control, 1840–1908' (1984).

nodes.label: The oases of the northwest
nodes.full: The northern oases — al-ʿUlā, Taymāʾ, Khaybar, Tabūk, Dūmat al-Jandal — lay under nominal Ottoman and sharifian authority but real tribal control: the ʿAnaza, the Balī, the Ḥuwayṭāt and the Rwala. The Syrian Hajj caravan was the one institution that reached them.
nodes.src: C. M. Doughty, 'Travels in Arabia Deserta' (1888); Alois Musil's later surveys of the northern Hejaz.

nodes.label: The Hajj-road forts and the amīr al-ḥajj
nodes.full: The Ottomans built and garrisoned a chain of forts along the Syrian pilgrim route — Tabūk, al-Muʿaẓẓam, al-ʿUlā, al-Ḥijr — each with a cistern, and paid the tribes a subsidy to let the caravan pass. The amīr al-ḥajj who led it from Damascus was a great Ottoman office.
nodes.src: Andrew Petersen, 'The Medieval and Ottoman Hajj Route in Jordan' (2012); the Ottoman fort inscriptions.

nodes.label: The sharifian civil wars
nodes.full: The Dhawū Zayd–Dhawū Barakāt feud and the wider quarrels of the Meccan sharifs, fought out over three centuries with Ottoman troops, Egyptian arbitration and tribal levies — the normal politics of the emirate.
nodes.src: Faroqhi (1994); the Ottoman military interventions recorded in the Hejaz chronicles.

nodes.label: The Saudi conquest of the Hejaz
nodes.full: The massacre at Ṭāʾif in 1802, the taking of Mecca and Medina, the demolition of the shrines and the closing of the Ottoman Hajj — the Wahhābī interlude as an armed occupation of the holiest ground in Islam.
nodes.src: Burckhardt, 'Notes on the Bedouins and Wahábys' (1830); the Saudi chronicles.

nodes.label: The Egyptian campaigns
nodes.full: Ṭūsūn's and Ibrāhīm Pasha's wars to retake the Hejaz and then to pursue the Saudis into Najd, fought with Egyptian artillery and levies against forces that had no answer to cannon.
nodes.src: Burckhardt (1829); the Egyptian campaign records.

nodes.label: The Jeddah massacre
nodes.full: A mob killed the British and French consuls and a number of Christian and local residents. A British warship bombarded the town and the Ottomans executed the ringleaders — an early, violent collision of the closed Hejaz with European power.
nodes.src: the British and French consular reports; Ulrike Freitag, 'A History of Jeddah' (2020).

nodes.label: The Bedouin and the Hajj
nodes.full: The raiding of the pilgrim caravans by the tribes of the route, the surra payments that bought passage, and the periodic disasters when a subsidy lapsed or a caravan was caught — a low, chronic war along the whole road, and a constant Ottoman expense.
nodes.src: Faroqhi (1994); the Ottoman correspondence on the tribal subsidies; the accounts of caravan attacks in the traveller literature.

nodes.label: The administration of a sacred province
nodes.full: The qāḍī of Mecca, a top post in the imperial religious hierarchy appointed from Istanbul for a year, the governor at Jeddah, the tax exemption, and a deliberate light touch — the Hejaz was administered as a trust to be protected, not a territory to be exploited.
nodes.src: Ochsenwald, 'Religion, Society, and the State in Arabia' (1984); Faroqhi (1994).

nodes.label: The organisation of the Hajj
nodes.full: The amīr al-ḥajj of Damascus and of Cairo, the fixed stages and forts, the subsidy to the tribes, the kiswa and the maḥmal — a logistical operation moving tens of thousands of people across the desert on a schedule, run by the Ottoman state.
nodes.src: Faroqhi, 'Pilgrims and Sultans' (1994); Jomier on the Egyptian maḥmal.

nodes.label: The waqf al-Ḥaramayn and the Sürre
nodes.full: Endowments across the empire dedicated to the two mosques, administered from Istanbul, plus the annual imperial gift of money and grain — the financial system that kept the Hejaz solvent, fed and loyal without taxing it.
nodes.src: the awqāf al-Ḥaramayn administration; Miriam Hoexter and Faroqhi on the endowment system.

nodes.label: The Egyptian interlude's reforms
nodes.full: Muḥammad ʿAlī's administration introduced a regular garrison, reorganised the Jeddah customs, and dealt more firmly with the sharifs and the tribes — a preview of the direct Ottoman rule that followed after 1840.
nodes.src: Ochsenwald (1984); the Egyptian administrative records.

nodes.label: Quarantine and the international regulation of the Hajj
nodes.full: After the 1865 cholera pandemic the international sanitary conferences imposed quarantine stations, medical inspection of pilgrim ships and limits on numbers — the first international regulation of a religious rite, and a European hand laid on the Ottoman Hejaz.
nodes.src: Valeska Huber, 'The Unification of the Globe by Disease? The International Sanitary Conferences on Cholera, 1851–1894'; the Kamaran quarantine records.

nodes.label: The Sunni establishment restored
nodes.full: After the Wahhābī interlude the Ottomans reinstated the four schools, the shrine visitation, the mawlid and the Sufi orders, and made the suppression of 'Wahhābism' a standing concern of the Mecca qāḍī and the governor.
nodes.src: Ochsenwald (1984); the Ottoman anti-Wahhābī fatwās and administrative circulars.

nodes.label: The Ḥaramayn as a hub of Islamic reform
nodes.full: Eighteenth- and nineteenth-century Mecca and Medina were where the founders of the great modern Sufi and reform movements met and studied — Aḥmad ibn Idrīs, the founders of the Sanūsiyya and the Khatmiyya, the Naqshbandī-Mujaddidī — a crossroads of ideas that spread from West Africa to Indonesia.
nodes.src: John Voll, 'Islam: Continuity and Change in the Modern World' (1982); R. S. O'Fahey, 'Enigmatic Saint: Ahmad ibn Idris' (1990).

nodes.label: The Jāwa colony and the global ʿulamāʾ
nodes.full: The resident scholarly communities of Mecca — the 'Jāwa' from the Malay world, the Indians, the Central Asians, the West Africans — grew huge in the 19th century, and the Meccan teachers of the Jāwa, above all Nawawī al-Bantanī, shaped the Islam of Southeast Asia.
nodes.src: C. Snouck Hurgronje, 'Mekka' (1888–89), on the Jāwa colony; Michael Laffan, 'Islamic Nationhood and Colonial Indonesia' (2003).

nodes.label: Pan-Islam and the Hejaz under Abdülhamid II
nodes.full: The sultan-caliph made the guardianship of the two holy cities and the welfare of the pilgrims the centrepiece of a pan-Islamic policy — the Sürre, the coming railway, the emphasis on the caliphal title — aimed at the Muslims of the British, French, Dutch and Russian empires.
nodes.src: Selim Deringil, 'The Well-Protected Domains' (1998); Kemal Karpat, 'The Politicization of Islam' (2001).

nodes.label: The Shiʿi and the vanished Jews of the north
nodes.full: The Nakhāwila Shiʿa of Medina, the Shiʿi and Zaydī pilgrims and residents, and — a memory by this period rather than a reality — the Jewish communities of Khaybar and the northern oases, long since gone, though 19th-century travellers still asked after them.
nodes.src: Werner Ende on the Nakhāwila; the traveller accounts (Doughty, Wallin) chasing the legend of the Jews of Khaybar.

nodes.label: The Ottoman Kaʿba and the Ḥaramayn
nodes.full: Murad IV's rebuilding of the Kaʿba after the flood of 1630 gave it the form it keeps today, and the Ottomans added domed colonnades, minarets and mosaics to the two mosques over four centuries — the last great imperial phase of building at the Ḥaramayn.
nodes.src: the Ottoman rebuilding accounts; the pre-modern photographs and plans of the Ḥaramayn.

nodes.label: Old Jeddah (al-Balad)
nodes.full: The tall coral-stone merchant houses with their carved wooden rawāshīn balconies, built on the Hajj and the Red Sea trade, gave old Jeddah a distinctive Red Sea urban form — now a UNESCO World Heritage site.
nodes.src: Ulrike Freitag, 'A History of Jeddah' (2020); the al-Balad UNESCO nomination file (2014).

nodes.label: The forts of the Hajj road
nodes.full: The squat Ottoman qalʿas along the Syrian and Egyptian pilgrim routes — each a fortified cistern and store — are the visible infrastructure of the imperial Hajj across the northwest desert, and among the best-preserved Ottoman military architecture in Arabia.
nodes.src: Petersen, 'The Medieval and Ottoman Hajj Route in Jordan' (2012); the Saudi surveys of the Darb al-Ḥajj al-Shāmī.

nodes.label: The pilgrim image, from the prayer book to the photograph
nodes.full: The enormously popular prayer book Dalāʾil al-Khayrāt, with its schematic paintings of the two mosques, was carried by pilgrims everywhere — and from the 1880s Snouck Hurgronje's photographs, taken with a Meccan assistant, became the first images of the holy city.
nodes.src: the Dalāʾil al-Khayrāt manuscript tradition; Snouck Hurgronje's 'Bilder-Atlas zu Mekka' (1889).

nodes.label: The music of the season
nodes.full: The drums and shawms of the maḥmal procession, the sharifs' court musicians at Ṭāʾif, and the work-songs of the water-carriers and the pilgrim guides — a limited public music in a city where the strict religious currents disapproved of it.
nodes.src: Snouck Hurgronje, 'Mekka' (1888–89), on Meccan music and the guilds; Lisa Urkevich, 'Music and Traditions of the Arabian Peninsula' (2015).

nodes.label: Burckhardt and Burton
nodes.full: Johann Ludwig Burckhardt's 'Travels in Arabia' (1829), the first accurate European account of the holy cities by a man who did the Hajj, and Richard Burton's 'Personal Narrative of a Pilgrimage to Al-Madinah and Meccah' (1855) — the founding texts of the Western literature on the Hejaz.
nodes.src: J. L. Burckhardt, 'Travels in Arabia' (1829); Richard F. Burton, 'Personal Narrative' (1855–56).

nodes.label: Doughty, Euting and the northwest
nodes.full: Charles Doughty's 'Travels in Arabia Deserta' (1888), mostly about the northern oases, and the 1883–84 journey of Charles Huber and Julius Euting that recovered the Aramaic Taymāʾ Stone — the northwest opened to Western scholarship, at the cost of Huber's murder near the coast in 1884.
nodes.src: C. M. Doughty, 'Travels in Arabia Deserta' (1888); Julius Euting, 'Tagbuch einer Reise in Inner-Arabien' (1896); the Taymāʾ Stone, now in the Louvre.

nodes.label: Snouck Hurgronje's Mekka
nodes.full: The Dutch orientalist lived in Mecca in 1884–85 and wrote 'Mekka', a detailed ethnography of the city, its scholars, its guilds and its Jāwa colony — the classic account of the late-Ottoman Hejaz, and, in service of Dutch colonial policy in the Indies, a work of intelligence.
nodes.src: C. Snouck Hurgronje, 'Mekka' (1888–89); Michael Laffan and others on its colonial context.

nodes.label: The medicine of the Hajj
nodes.full: The epidemiological literature that grew from the 19th-century cholera pandemics — the Ottoman and Egyptian sanitary services, the reports to the international conferences, the debate over whether to restrict the pilgrimage — made the Hajj a subject of modern public health.
nodes.src: Adrien Proust, 'Essai sur l'hygiène internationale' (1873); the proceedings of the International Sanitary Conferences (1866, 1874, 1885, 1894).

nodes.label: The Hajj as the whole economy
nodes.full: Pilgrim spending, the hereditary Meccan guilds of guides, camel-brokers and water-carriers, the Jeddah customs, and the imperial subsidies — Mecca produced almost nothing and lived entirely on the pilgrimage and the piety of the empire.
nodes.src: Snouck Hurgronje, 'Mekka' (1888–89); Ochsenwald (1984).

nodes.label: Jeddah, the Red Sea port
nodes.full: The harbour handled the sea pilgrims and a transit trade in coffee, spices, pearls and grain between the Indian Ocean, Egypt and the Levant. Its merchant houses — Indian, Hadrami, local — were the Hejaz's real capitalists.
nodes.src: Ulrike Freitag, 'A History of Jeddah: The Gate to Mecca in the Nineteenth and Twentieth Centuries' (2020).

nodes.label: The steamship Hajj
nodes.full: From the 1850s and especially after the Suez Canal in 1869, steamships carried pilgrims to Jeddah in tens of thousands from India, the Dutch East Indies and the Ottoman ports — a mass pilgrimage that transformed the scale, the economics and the danger of the Hajj.
nodes.src: John Slight, 'The British Empire and the Hajj, 1865–1956' (2015); Eric Tagliacozzo, 'The Longest Journey' (2013).

nodes.label: The slave trade through Jeddah
nodes.full: Enslaved Africans from Sudan and Ethiopia, shipped via Suakin and Massawa, were sold at Jeddah and Mecca, some to pilgrims, some manumitted at the holy sites. British and half-hearted Ottoman measures from the 1850s reduced but did not end the traffic before 1900.
nodes.src: Ehud Toledano, 'The Ottoman Slave Trade and Its Suppression' (1982); William Gervase Clarence-Smith, 'Islam and the Abolition of Slavery' (2006).

nodes.label: The forts and cisterns of the pilgrim road
nodes.full: The Ottoman qalʿas and their stone reservoirs along the Syrian route were the water and security infrastructure without which the caravan could not have crossed the northwest desert — the one thing the empire built and maintained in the region.
nodes.src: Petersen (2012); the Saudi and Jordanian surveys of the Ottoman Hajj forts.

nodes.label: Steam, telegraph and quarantine
nodes.full: The steamship that remade the Hajj, the telegraph line that reached Jeddah and Mecca in the 1880s, and the quarantine stations and disinfection plants at Kamaran and al-Ṭūr — the Hejaz wired into the imperial and international grid.
nodes.src: Deringil, 'The Well-Protected Domains' (1998); Valeska Huber on the sanitary infrastructure.

nodes.label: The Hejaz Railway begins
nodes.full: Abdülhamid II authorised in 1900 a railway from Damascus to Medina, funded by donations from Muslims worldwide and built by the Ottoman army — a project of pilgrimage, strategy and pan-Islamic prestige, begun at the very end of this folio.
nodes.src: William Ochsenwald, 'The Hijaz Railroad' (1980); the railway's completion to Medina in 1908 belongs to the next folio.

nodes.label: Istanbul and the guardianship
nodes.full: The Ottoman sultan-caliph's guardianship of the two holy cities was the empire's most valuable non-material asset — the basis of the caliphal claim, the argument for its leadership of the Sunni world, and, under Abdülhamid, a lever against the European powers.
nodes.src: Deringil (1998); Karpat, 'The Politicization of Islam' (2001).

nodes.label: The Hajj as the umma's assembly
nodes.full: The pilgrimage kept its role as the great annual meeting — of scholars, books, goods and disease, and increasingly in the 19th century of anti-colonial politics, which the British, Dutch and French watched closely through their Jeddah consulates.
nodes.src: Slight, 'The British Empire and the Hajj' (2015); Tagliacozzo, 'The Longest Journey' (2013).

nodes.label: Europe reaches the Hejaz
nodes.full: The Jeddah consulates, the sanitary regime, the naval bombardment of 1858 and the disguised travellers — the beginning of a European presence in and pressure on a region that had been closed to non-Muslims for a thousand years.
nodes.src: Freitag, 'A History of Jeddah' (2020); the consular archives.

nodes.label: The Meccan networks of the colonised Muslim world
nodes.full: The Jāwa, Indian and West African communities at Mecca were channels back to the Dutch East Indies, British India and French Africa, carrying reformist and, later, anti-colonial ideas home with the returning pilgrims — a flow the colonial powers tried and failed to monitor.
nodes.src: Snouck Hurgronje, 'Mekka' (1888–89); Laffan, 'Islamic Nationhood and Colonial Indonesia' (2003).

nodes.label: The northwest as tribal borderland
nodes.full: The oases and routes of the northwest lay between the Ottoman Hejaz, the sharifate, the Rashīdī and Saudi Najd, and the confederations of the Syrian desert — claimed by all and governed by none, crossed twice a year by the pilgrimage.
nodes.src: Doughty (1888); the later British and Ottoman surveys of the northern Hejaz frontier.

nodes.label: The most sacred and least profitable province
nodes.full: The Ottomans held the Hejaz at a permanent loss, for the legitimacy the guardianship conferred. It paid no tax, cost the Sürre and the caravan subsidies, and its politics were managed by payment rather than by force.
nodes.src: Ochsenwald (1984); Faroqhi (1994).

nodes.label: The Wahhābī interlude as a lasting lesson
nodes.full: The 1803–1818 Saudi occupation of the Ḥaramayn showed how fragile the guardianship was, and made the containment of the Wahhābī–Saudi movement a fixed priority — Ottoman, then Egyptian, then British — for a century.
nodes.src: Ochsenwald (1984); the recurring Ottoman anxiety about a second Saudi advance.

nodes.label: Steam remakes the Hajj
nodes.full: Within a generation the pilgrimage went from a caravan of thousands to a shipborne mass of hundreds of thousands — bigger, cheaper, more global, and a recurring vector of cholera (some fifteen thousand dead at Mecca in 1865) that made the Hejaz an object of international regulation.
nodes.src: Valeska Huber on the sanitary conferences; the WHO retrospectives on Hajj cholera. Casualty figures are contemporary estimates.

nodes.label: The thread continues — the railway, the Sharif Hussein and the Revolt
nodes.full: The folio ends in 1900 with the Hejaz Railway authorised and the Vilayet in place. The railway's completion to Medina in 1908, Sharif Hussein's appointment, the Arab Revolt of 1916 and the short-lived Hashemite kingdom are the next folio.
nodes.src: a forward reference: hejaz-1900-1925 (the railway, the Arab Revolt and the Kingdom of the Hejaz) is planned but not yet built.

nodes.label: The mutawwifūn and the guilds
nodes.full: The hereditary guild of pilgrim guides, each family licensed to serve pilgrims from a particular country, and the guilds of camel-brokers, water-carriers and porters — a whole urban economy and society organised around receiving the Hajj.
nodes.src: Snouck Hurgronje, 'Mekka' (1888–89), on the guild system; later studies of the mutawwif institution.

nodes.label: The Jāwa, Indian and African communities
nodes.full: The resident foreigners of Mecca — students, merchants, freed slaves, exiles — many of whom never left, formed settled communities that Snouck Hurgronje mapped and that made Mecca one of the most cosmopolitan cities on earth.
nodes.src: Snouck Hurgronje, 'Mekka' (1888–89); Tagliacozzo and Toorawa (eds), 'The Hajj: Pilgrimage in Islam' (2016).

nodes.label: The slave market and manumission
nodes.full: The Jeddah and Mecca slave markets, the enslaved Africans who arrived with the pilgrim traffic, and the custom of freeing a slave at the holy sites — the same ground where slavery was practised was where, ritually, it was undone.
nodes.src: Toledano, 'The Ottoman Slave Trade' (1982); Clarence-Smith, 'Islam and the Abolition of Slavery' (2006).

nodes.label: Women on the Hajj
nodes.full: Women came in growing numbers, especially by steamship, under the maḥram rules; the sanitary regime's inspection of women pilgrims caused particular scandal; and the few surviving accounts by women pilgrims are a rare window on the experience of the Hajj.
nodes.src: the accounts of women pilgrims (e.g. Lady Evelyn Cobbold, later; the earlier Ottoman women's Hajj memoirs); Marjo Buitelaar on women and the Hajj.
